sections.title: Surgery, immobility and clot risk
sections.text: Tell the surgical and oncology teams that you take tamoxifen. They decide whether any temporary interruption is needed; there is no automatic fixed interruption for everyone.

sections.title: Bleeding and eye symptoms

sections.title: Review all medicines
sections.text: Review prescriptions, supplements and over-the-counter products, including antidepressants, blood thinners and hormone preparations. evidence.title: Why tamoxifen is offered
evidence.population: People with oestrogen-receptor-positive early breast cancer in randomized studies.
evidence.interpretation: Taking the planned course after early breast cancer reduces the chance of the cancer returning and lowers the risk of dying from breast cancer. A longer course may bring further benefit for some people.
evidence.limitations: The size of the benefit depends on your cancer, previous treatment and remaining risk. Early-breast study results do not predict how an individual with advanced breast cancer will respond. Longer treatment also carries risks and should be reviewed with the team.

items.title: Early-breast follow-up
items.text: After curative treatment, annual mammography is generally used for remaining breast tissue: both breasts after conservation or the opposite breast after unilateral mastectomy. The mastectomy side is not routinely mammographed. Routine CT, bone scans and tumour markers are not recommended for asymptomatic early-breast surveillance. New symptoms need assessment between appointments.

items.title: Surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy
items.text: In an early-breast pathway, chemotherapy, if indicated, precedes endocrine treatment. Surgery and its pathology guide adjuvant choices. Postoperative radiotherapy is usually delivered after recovery and any adjuvant chemotherapy; aromatase inhibitors may overlap radiotherapy under the agreed plan. Tamoxifen timing around radiotherapy is agreed by the treating teams. None of these additional treatments is automatically required by an endocrine prescription.

items.title: Advanced-disease scans
items.text: For advanced breast cancer, response assessment is generally every two to four months, adapted to disease pace, sites, symptoms and treatment. Indolent disease may be reviewed less often; new symptoms can prompt earlier scans. The team chooses the imaging method; this is not a universal three-month CT chest/abdomen/pelvis order.

items.title: Tumour markers
items.text: Tumour markers may supplement imaging and clinical assessment in advanced disease if they are informative, especially if elevated at baseline. They do not replace scans, and a marker change alone should not determine treatment failure. There is no universal fixed marker timetable.

items.title: Menopause, pregnancy and contraception
items.text: Tamoxifen is not contraception. Discuss an effective non-hormonal method during treatment and for nine months after stopping, where relevant. Absent periods do not prove infertility. Pregnancy and breastfeeding are excluded from this NCCP pathway.

questions.q: What if side effects make me want to stop?
questions.a: Contact the team early. Help with symptoms or a review of the endocrine plan may make treatment easier. Do not wait until you miss several doses to ask for support.

Tissue-specific action explains uterine stimulation and differing pre/postmenopausal bone effects.

evidence.trial: EBCTCG; ATLAS; supportive aTTom duration context
evidence.population: ER-positive early breast cancer; initial adjuvant treatment and extension decisions are distinct.
evidence.comparison: EBCTCG: about 5 years versus none. ATLAS/aTTom: continue to 10 years versus stop at 5 years.
evidence.applicability: NCCP00253 also includes advanced disease; these adjuvant results do not provide a metastatic survival estimate.

endpoints.metric: ATLAS overall mortality in the ER-positive population
endpoints.interpretation: Overall mortality was lower with extended treatment in ATLAS; not a fixed-time survival percentage.
endpoints.definition: Death from any cause after randomization at completion of 5 years tamoxifen.
endpoints.limitations: Different endpoint from breast-cancer mortality; use the correct denominator and population.

evidence.qualitative_result: EBCTCG 2011: ER-positive recurrence rate ratios 0.53 during years 0–4 and 0.68 during years 5–9; breast-cancer mortality fell by about one-third through 15 years. ATLAS years 5–14 recurrence was 21.4% versus 25.1% and breast-cancer mortality 12.2% versus 15.0%. These are recurrence and cause-specific mortality results, not DFS or OS percentages.
limitations: Absolute benefit depends on recurrence risk.
aTTom corroborates recurrence reduction but its overall mortality comparison was not significant (P=.1); it included many ER-untested patients and is sourced here to a meeting abstract.
Extension is not automatic for everyone; benefit and harm populations in ATLAS differ.
evidence.harms: ATLAS: extended treatment increased pulmonary embolus risk (RR 1.87) and endometrial cancer (years 5–14: 3.1% versus 1.6%).

evidence_records.population: 20 randomized early-breast trials; 21, 457 women overall; ER-positive efficacy analysis 10, 645.
evidence_records.comparison: About 5 years adjuvant tamoxifen versus no tamoxifen.

outcomes.interpretation: Earlier recurrence gains persist after treatment ends; the later near-unity rate ratio is not loss of the prior benefit.
Roughly one-third lower breast-cancer mortality through 15 years; do not label this as overall survival.

limitations: Absolute benefit depends on baseline recurrence risk. Relative effects are not absolute risk reductions.
ER-negative disease showed little or no effect. This historical adjuvant comparison does not quantify metastatic benefit or rank modern endocrine combinations.

evidence_records.population: 12, 894 randomized after 5 years of tamoxifen; breast-cancer efficacy among 6, 846 ER-positive women; harms among all receptor groups.
evidence_records.comparison: Continue to 10 years versus stop at 5 years.

outcomes.interpretation: Overall mortality was reduced in the ER-positive efficacy analysis; these event counts are not a fixed-time survival percentage.

evidence_records.harms: Pulmonary embolus RR 1.87 (95% CI 1.13–3.07); endometrial cancer years 5–14: 3.1% versus 1.6%.
limitations: Benefit became more apparent after year 10. Longer treatment is an individual risk–benefit decision.
Do not conflate efficacy population with all-receptor safety analysis or convert cause-specific mortality into OS.

patient.title: Fulvestrant · injections every 4 weeks
patient.context_label: Postmenopausal ER-positive locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer
patient.schedule_summary: NCCP schedule: 500 mg on Days 1 and 15 of the first 28-day cycle, then Day 1 of each 28-day cycle. This means Day 29 next, then every 28 days.
patient.purpose: The aim is to control advanced hormone-sensitive breast cancer and its symptoms, with response and tolerability reviewed before continuing.
patient.indication_text: This NCCP monotherapy pathway covers postmenopausal women with ER-positive locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer that has relapsed or progressed on or after adjuvant anti-oestrogen treatment. Fulvestrant prescribed with capivasertib or a CDK4/6 medicine follows a separate combination regimen.
patient.administration_text: Each usual 500 mg dose is given as two 5 mL injections, one in each buttock, slowly over one to two minutes per injection. This is not an intravenous infusion; no port or pump is needed for fulvestrant itself.
patient.monitoring_summary: Before treatment, check blood count, kidney and liver function, the menopausal and treatment history, pregnancy exclusion and bleeding risk. Before injections, tell staff about anticoagulants, bruising, bleeding or previous nerve symptoms. Repeat liver tests when indicated; scans follow the agreed cancer-control plan. Tell anyone ordering an oestrogen blood test that you receive fulvestrant because some tests can give a misleadingly high result.

evidence.title: Why fulvestrant is offered
evidence.population: Postmenopausal people with hormone-sensitive advanced breast cancer studied in endocrine-treatment trials.
evidence.primary_endpoint: Control of cancer progression and survival, evaluated separately.
evidence.interpretation: Fulvestrant can help control advanced hormone-sensitive breast cancer. Studies support the usual treatment schedule, while the choice of treatment depends on previous endocrine therapy and the individual cancer.
evidence.limitations: A study comparing fulvestrant doses does not show that monotherapy is better than modern combination treatment. A separate study in people who had not received endocrine therapy found longer control of progression but no proven overall-survival advantage over anastrozole. These findings do not predict an individual outcome.

chapters.title: The treatment being discussed

items.title: Who this information covers
items.text: This NCCP monotherapy pathway covers postmenopausal women with ER-positive locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer that has relapsed or progressed on or after adjuvant anti-oestrogen treatment. Fulvestrant prescribed with capivasertib or a CDK4/6 medicine follows a separate combination regimen.

items.title: Medicine and schedule
items.text: NCCP schedule: 500 mg on Days 1 and 15 of the first 28-day cycle, then Day 1 of each 28-day cycle. This means Day 29 next, then every 28 days. Each usual 500 mg dose is given as two 5 mL injections, one in each buttock, slowly over one to two minutes per injection. This is not an intravenous infusion; no port or pump is needed for fulvestrant itself.

items.text: Before treatment, check blood count, kidney and liver function, the menopausal and treatment history, pregnancy exclusion and bleeding risk. items.title: Advanced-disease scans
items.text: For advanced breast cancer, response assessment is generally every two to four months, adapted to disease pace, sites, symptoms and treatment. Indolent disease may be reviewed less often; new symptoms can prompt earlier scans. The team chooses the imaging method; this is not a universal three-month CT chest/abdomen/pelvis order.

items.title: Tumour markers
items.text: Tumour markers may supplement imaging and clinical assessment in advanced disease if they are informative, especially if elevated at baseline. They do not replace scans, and a marker change alone should not determine treatment failure. There is no universal fixed marker timetable.

items.title: Menopause, pregnancy and contraception
items.text: Where relevant, effective contraception is needed during treatment and for two years after the final dose under the EMA product information. Pregnancy and breastfeeding are excluded.

questions.q: When are the injections given?
questions.a: The usual schedule is Day 1, Day 15 and Day 29, then every 28 days. The first month includes an extra loading visit. Follow your clinic appointments; contact the team if a visit is missed.

questions.q: When are bloods, ECGs or echoes needed?
questions.a: Before treatment, check blood count, kidney and liver function, the menopausal and treatment history, pregnancy exclusion and bleeding risk. Before injections, tell staff about anticoagulants, bruising, bleeding or previous nerve symptoms. Repeat liver tests when indicated; scans follow the agreed cancer-control plan. Tell anyone ordering an oestrogen blood test that you receive fulvestrant because some tests can give a misleadingly high result. There is no routine ECG or echo schedule for fulvestrant alone; a companion medicine may need additional checks.

questions.q: Which scans apply to me?
questions.a: For advanced breast cancer, response assessment is generally every two to four months, adapted to disease pace, sites, symptoms and treatment. Indolent disease may be reviewed less often; new symptoms can prompt earlier scans. The team chooses the imaging method; this is not a universal three-month CT chest/abdomen/pelvis order.

questions.q: What is my bone-health plan?
questions.a: Assess personal fracture and osteoporosis risk. Fulvestrant does not carry an automatic AI DXA timetable; agree testing and repeat intervals when indicated.

questions.q: How long will treatment continue?
questions.a: Continue while the treatment is beneficial and tolerated, with planned response reviews. There is no fixed adjuvant five-year course on this card.

questions.q: Do I need a port or home pump?
questions.a: No port or home infusion pump is needed for this medicine itself. Any separately prescribed medicine has its own access requirements.

questions.q: Is this the same plan as capivasertib with fulvestrant?
questions.a: No. The injections are part of both plans, but capivasertib adds its own tablet schedule, selection requirements, blood-sugar checks and side-effect care. Use the full combination plan if both are prescribed.

questions.q: Why might an oestrogen test need checking?
questions.a: Fulvestrant can interfere with some laboratory tests and make the result look higher than it is. Tell the team about treatment so they can check the test method before making a treatment decision.

rationale.summary: Fulvestrant antagonizes and degrades the oestrogen receptor, providing a different endocrine mechanism from lowering oestrogen production. The initial loading schedule establishes exposure before 28-day maintenance. The NCCP00361 card is monotherapy in a specified post-adjuvant anti-oestrogen setting.

agents.mechanism: Reduces the oestrogen available to stimulate cancer cells
agents.explanation: Anastrozole blocks aromatase, an enzyme that makes oestrogen in fat and other tissues after menopause. It does not reliably switch off functioning ovaries; any ovarian-suppression treatment needs a separate prescription and checks.

chapters.title: The treatment being discussed
chapters.intro: After early breast cancer treatment, endocrine therapy reduces the risk of recurrence. In advanced disease, the aim is to control cancer and symptoms. Your setting determines the duration and follow-up.

items.title: Who this information covers
items.text: Postmenopausal hormone-sensitive breast cancer in the NCCP adjuvant, switch-after-tamoxifen or advanced settings. The exact receptor and prior-treatment criteria remain a prescribing decision.

items.title: Medicine and schedule
items.text: Take anastrozole once daily continuously. There is no planned week off. The treatment setting determines the intended duration. Swallow the tablet whole with water, with or without food. Do not replace a missed or vomited dose; resume the next scheduled dose.

items.title: Review and duration
items.text: Swallow the tablet whole with water, with or without food. Do not replace a missed or vomited dose; resume the next scheduled dose. A change from tamoxifen does not automatically restart the whole treatment clock. Ask which earlier treatment counts towards your plan.

items.title: Individual risks and support
items.text: A functioning premenopausal ovarian state is not compatible with AI monotherapy. Severe hepatic impairment is not recommended by NCCP; moderate impairment requires caution. Confirm menopausal status rather than assuming that absent periods after chemotherapy mean permanent menopause. Any ovarian-suppression treatment must have its own prescribed schedule.

chapters.title: Checks throughout treatment
chapters.intro: Your team arranges tests and explains the results. A planned check is not confirmation that it has been completed.

items.title: Treatment-specific checks
items.text: FBC, renal and liver profile. Confirm menopause; hormone tests may be needed if it is uncertain. Assess fracture risk and baseline bone density, particularly for adjuvant AI treatment. The NICE adjuvant baseline-DXA recommendation has an exception for patients already receiving adjuvant bisphosphonates. Assess symptoms, adherence and bone health at reviews. Repeat lipids and other blood tests when clinically indicated. Bone-density timing follows baseline results and fracture risk.

items.title: Heart checks
items.text: ECG or other heart tests depend on symptoms and personal risk; this medicine alone does not require a routine HER2-style echocardiogram schedule.

items.title: Bone health
items.text: Offer baseline DXA when starting an adjuvant aromatase inhibitor if not already receiving adjuvant bisphosphonates; assess fracture risk and relevant previous results. Under the 2025 joint guidance, patients with a T-score above −2.0 and no additional risk factors generally have risk and bone density reassessed every one to two years. Patients on bone-protective treatment generally have BMD reassessed about every two years. Fracture, substantial bone loss or a change in risk can require earlier review. The clinician selects the interval and any bone treatment; these are not automatic yearly scans for everyone.

chapters.title: Your setting changes the pathway
chapters.intro: Choose the pathway that your team has confirmed; these are not all extra treatments you must have.

items.title: Early-breast follow-up
items.text: After curative treatment, annual mammography is generally used for remaining breast tissue: both breasts after conservation or the opposite breast after unilateral mastectomy. The mastectomy side is not routinely mammographed. Routine CT, bone scans and tumour markers are not recommended for asymptomatic early-breast surveillance. New symptoms need assessment between appointments.

items.title: Surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy
items.text: In an early-breast pathway, chemotherapy, if indicated, precedes endocrine treatment. Surgery and its pathology guide adjuvant choices. Postoperative radiotherapy is usually delivered after recovery and any adjuvant chemotherapy; aromatase inhibitors may overlap radiotherapy under the agreed plan. Tamoxifen timing around radiotherapy is agreed by the treating teams. None of these additional treatments is automatically required by an endocrine prescription.

items.title: Advanced-disease scans
items.text: For advanced breast cancer, response assessment is generally every two to four months, adapted to disease pace, sites, symptoms and treatment. Indolent disease may be reviewed less often; new symptoms can prompt earlier scans. The team chooses the imaging method; this is not a universal three-month CT chest/abdomen/pelvis order.

items.title: Tumour markers
items.text: Tumour markers may supplement imaging and clinical assessment in advanced disease if they are informative, especially if elevated at baseline. They do not replace scans, and a marker change alone should not determine treatment failure. There is no universal fixed marker timetable.

items.title: Menopause, pregnancy and contraception
items.text: Confirm menopausal status rather than assuming that absent periods after chemotherapy mean permanent menopause. Any ovarian-suppression treatment must have its own prescribed schedule.

questions.q: How long will treatment continue?
questions.a: After early breast cancer treatment, the team sets the intended total endocrine treatment length, taking account of any earlier tamoxifen. A course of several years may later be reviewed for extension according to recurrence risk, tolerance and bone health. Advanced-disease treatment is reviewed according to benefit and tolerance. A review date is not an automatic stop date.

questions.q: Do I need a port or home pump?
questions.a: No port or home infusion pump is needed for this medicine itself. Any separately prescribed medicine has its own access requirements.

questions.q: Can I use HRT, vaginal oestrogen or supplements?
questions.a: Check with the oncology team before starting any hormone-containing treatment, including vaginal oestrogen, or any new medicine or supplement. Some can oppose this treatment or change how it works. The team can suggest symptom treatments and decide whether specialist review is needed.

questions.q: What if periods return or menopause is uncertain?
questions.a: Tell the team promptly about a return of periods or new vaginal bleeding. No periods after chemotherapy does not always mean the ovaries have permanently stopped working. Hormone blood tests may be needed. Ovarian suppression, if prescribed, has its own schedule and monitoring.

questions.q: What should I do if symptoms make tablets difficult to continue?
questions.a: Tell the team early about joint pain, hot flushes, sleep, vaginal or sexual symptoms, fatigue or missed tablets. Support, a supervised break or a change of medicine may be possible. Agree the plan with the prescriber rather than changing or stopping treatment yourself.

questions.q: Do I need calcium and vitamin D?
questions.a: The NCCP regimen advises daily calcium and vitamin D supplementation. Ask the team or pharmacist to confirm the suitable product and dose, taking account of your diet, blood results, kidney health and any supplements you already take. Bone-protective medicines and bone-density checks follow your individual fracture-risk plan.

evidence.trial: ATAC: ten-year analysis of initial adjuvant anastrozole versus tamoxifen
evidence.population: ATAC: ten-year analysis of initial adjuvant anastrozole versus tamoxifen: Postmenopausal early breast cancer; 6,241 women in the two monotherapy groups, including 5,216 with hormone-receptor-positive disease; median follow-up 120 months.
evidence.comparison: ATAC: ten-year analysis of initial adjuvant anastrozole versus tamoxifen: Anastrozole 1 mg daily for 5 years versus Tamoxifen 20 mg daily for 5 years
evidence.applicability: Initial adjuvant treatment; not a metastatic or neoadjuvant benefit estimate.
evidence.qualitative_result: ATAC: ten-year analysis of initial adjuvant anastrozole versus tamoxifen: In the HR-positive subgroup, DFS HR 0.86 (95% CI 0.78–0.95) and time-to-recurrence HR 0.79 (0.70–0.89) favoured anastrozole. Absolute recurrence difference at 10 years was 4.3 percentage points. Overall mortality was not significantly different: HR 0.95 (0.84–1.06).

sources.label: ATAC: ten-year analysis of initial adjuvant anastrozole versus tamoxifen

limitations: Adjuvant results cannot supply an advanced-disease prognosis or authorise AI monotherapy with functioning ovaries. Fractures were more frequent during active anastrozole treatment. The trial is not evidence for restarting a complete five-year course after a tamoxifen switch.
evidence.harms: Bone loss, fracture and musculoskeletal symptoms need individual review; compare the actual options in the relevant treatment setting.

agents.mechanism: Reduces the oestrogen available to stimulate cancer cells
agents.explanation: Letrozole blocks aromatase, reducing the oestrogen made in tissues after menopause and the stimulation of hormone-sensitive breast cancer cells. This can be useful in different settings, but a before-surgery course needs response and surgical reviews, while treatment after surgery has a planned total duration. It does not reliably switch off functioning ovaries; ovarian suppression needs its own treatment plan.

items.title: Who this information covers
items.text: Letrozole is used for selected postmenopausal hormone-sensitive breast cancer before surgery, after surgery, as extended treatment or for advanced disease. Before-surgery treatment also depends on HER2 results, whether chemotherapy is suitable and whether surgery should happen immediately; the team checks these details.

items.title: Medicine and schedule
items.text: Take letrozole once daily continuously. The prescriber confirms whether the aim is before surgery, after surgery, extended adjuvant treatment or advanced-disease control. Take with or without food. Take a forgotten dose when remembered unless the next dose is within about two to three hours; then skip it. Do not take two doses together.

items.title: Review and duration
items.text: Take with or without food. Take a forgotten dose when remembered unless the next dose is within about two to three hours; then skip it. Do not take two doses together. A before-surgery response review, an adjuvant duration review and an advanced-disease scan answer different questions; use the milestones for your setting.

items.title: Individual risks and support
items.text: The usual prescription is once daily, but severe liver impairment can require a different frequency. Use the frequency on your prescription and confirm any change with the prescriber or pharmacist. An already reduced or unusual schedule must be reviewed before it is changed. Confirmed menopause is needed for this monotherapy; any ovarian suppression has its own prescription and monitoring.

chapters.title: Checks throughout treatment
chapters.intro: Your team arranges tests and explains the results. A planned check is not confirmation that it has been completed.

items.title: Treatment-specific checks
items.text: FBC, renal and liver profile; confirm menopause with hormone tests when uncertain. Assess fracture risk and baseline bone density, particularly for adjuvant AI treatment. The NICE adjuvant baseline-DXA recommendation has an exception for patients already receiving adjuvant bisphosphonates. FBC, renal / liver profile and lipids when clinically indicated. Review bone density during treatment and after treatment according to bone risk. Neoadjuvant response and surgical planning need explicit review milestones.

items.title: Heart checks
items.text: ECG or other heart tests depend on symptoms and personal risk; this medicine alone does not require a routine HER2-style echocardiogram schedule.

items.title: Bone health
items.text: Offer baseline DXA when starting an adjuvant aromatase inhibitor if not already receiving adjuvant bisphosphonates; assess fracture risk and relevant previous results. Under the 2025 joint guidance, patients with a T-score above −2.0 and no additional risk factors generally have risk and bone density reassessed every one to two years. Patients on bone-protective treatment generally have BMD reassessed about every two years. Fracture, substantial bone loss or a change in risk can require earlier review. The clinician selects the interval and any bone treatment; these are not automatic yearly scans for everyone.

chapters.title: Your setting changes the pathway
chapters.intro: Choose the pathway that your team has confirmed; these are not all extra treatments you must have.

items.title: Early-breast follow-up
items.text: After curative treatment, annual mammography is generally used for remaining breast tissue: both breasts after conservation or the opposite breast after unilateral mastectomy. The mastectomy side is not routinely mammographed. Routine CT, bone scans and tumour markers are not recommended for asymptomatic early-breast surveillance. New symptoms need assessment between appointments.

items.title: Surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy
items.text: In an early-breast pathway, chemotherapy, if indicated, precedes endocrine treatment. Surgery and its pathology guide adjuvant choices. Postoperative radiotherapy is usually delivered after recovery and any adjuvant chemotherapy; aromatase inhibitors may overlap radiotherapy under the agreed plan. Tamoxifen timing around radiotherapy is agreed by the treating teams. None of these additional treatments is automatically required by an endocrine prescription.

items.title: Advanced-disease scans
items.text: For advanced breast cancer, response assessment is generally every two to four months, adapted to disease pace, sites, symptoms and treatment. Indolent disease may be reviewed less often; new symptoms can prompt earlier scans. The team chooses the imaging method; this is not a universal three-month CT chest/abdomen/pelvis order.

items.title: Tumour markers
items.text: Tumour markers may supplement imaging and clinical assessment in advanced disease if they are informative, especially if elevated at baseline. They do not replace scans, and a marker change alone should not determine treatment failure. There is no universal fixed marker timetable.

items.title: Menopause, pregnancy and contraception
items.text: AIs alone require a confirmed postmenopausal endocrine state. Ovarian suppression is a separate treatment plan and must not be assumed from this card.

questions.q: Do I have a treatment-free week?
questions.a: Letrozole is usually taken every day without a planned treatment-free week. Some people have a different prescribed frequency because of liver problems. Follow your own prescription and check before changing it.

questions.q: How long will treatment continue?
questions.a: For the NCCP neoadjuvant pathway, reassess response during a four-to-eight-month course and discuss surgery or alternatives if response is inadequate. Adjuvant / extended duration and advanced-disease continuation follow separate plans.

questions.q: Do I need a port or home pump?
questions.a: No port or home infusion pump is needed for this medicine itself. Any separately prescribed medicine has its own access requirements.

questions.q: Can I use HRT, vaginal oestrogen or supplements?
questions.a: Check with the oncology team before starting any hormone-containing treatment, including vaginal oestrogen, or any new medicine or supplement. Some can oppose this treatment or change how it works. The team can suggest symptom treatments and decide whether specialist review is needed.

questions.q: What if periods return or menopause is uncertain?
questions.a: Tell the team promptly about a return of periods or new vaginal bleeding. No periods after chemotherapy does not always mean the ovaries have permanently stopped working. Hormone blood tests may be needed. Ovarian suppression, if prescribed, has its own schedule and monitoring.

questions.q: What should I do if symptoms make tablets difficult to continue?
questions.a: Tell the team early about joint pain, hot flushes, sleep, vaginal or sexual symptoms, fatigue or missed tablets. Support, a supervised break or a change of medicine may be possible. Agree the plan with the prescriber rather than changing or stopping treatment yourself.

questions.q: Will before-surgery treatment delay my operation automatically?
questions.a: No. Your team agrees when to assess the response and when surgery should take place. The NCCP pathway describes a course of about four to eight months to allow tumour reduction; inadequate response requires a discussion of surgery or another treatment. New symptoms or changes should be reported sooner.

questions.q: Do I need calcium and vitamin D?
questions.a: The NCCP regimen advises daily calcium and vitamin D supplementation. Ask the team or pharmacist to confirm the suitable product and dose, taking account of your diet, blood results, kidney health and any supplements you already take. Bone-protective medicines and bone-density checks follow your individual fracture-risk plan.

evidence.trial: BIG 1-98: long-term follow-up of letrozole versus tamoxifen; MA.17: extended adjuvant letrozole following tamoxifen; P024: preoperative letrozole versus tamoxifen
evidence.population: BIG 1-98: long-term follow-up of letrozole versus tamoxifen: Postmenopausal HR-positive early breast cancer; 8,010 randomized overall, including a 4,922-patient monotherapy comparison. Long-term follow-up was available from participating centres for 3,833 of 4,433 eligible patients; median follow-up 12.6 years. MA.17: extended adjuvant letrozole following tamoxifen: 5,187 postmenopausal women after approximately 5 years of tamoxifen; double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trial, median follow-up 30 months at this updated report. P024: preoperative letrozole versus tamoxifen: 337 postmenopausal women with untreated ER- and/or PgR-positive primary breast cancer initially unsuitable for breast-conserving surgery; randomized double-blind comparison.
evidence.comparison: BIG 1-98: long-term follow-up of letrozole versus tamoxifen: Letrozole 2.5 mg daily for 5 years versus Tamoxifen 20 mg daily for 5 years MA.17: extended adjuvant letrozole following tamoxifen: Letrozole 2.5 mg daily, planned for 5 years versus Placebo P024: preoperative letrozole versus tamoxifen: Letrozole 2.5 mg daily for 4 months versus Tamoxifen 20 mg daily for 4 months
evidence.applicability: Initial adjuvant treatment; latest long-term primary report identified in this audit. Extended adjuvant treatment after tamoxifen. Neoadjuvant treatment, distinct from adjuvant recurrence prevention and advanced-disease control.
evidence.qualitative_result: BIG 1-98: long-term follow-up of letrozole versus tamoxifen: At median 12.6 years, the DFS estimate for letrozole versus tamoxifen was HR 0.91 (95% CI 0.81–1.01); this confidence interval includes no difference. The latest report therefore must not be described as a statistically significant long-term DFS advantage on the strength of the earlier 8.7-year estimate. MA.17: extended adjuvant letrozole following tamoxifen: DFS HR 0.58 (95% CI 0.45–0.76; P<0.001) and distant DFS HR 0.60 (0.43–0.84; P=0.002) favoured letrozole. Overall survival was not significantly improved across the whole randomized population: HR 0.82 (0.57–1.19; P=0.30). P024: preoperative letrozole versus tamoxifen: Clinical response was 55% versus 36% (P<0.001), favouring letrozole. Breast-conserving surgery occurred in 45% versus 35% (P=0.022).

patient.title: Exemestane · daily hormone therapy
patient.context_label: Postmenopausal ER-positive breast cancer after prior endocrine treatment
patient.schedule_summary: Take exemestane once daily continuously, preferably after a meal. There is no planned week off. Confirm the prior-treatment and duration plan.
patient.purpose: After early breast cancer treatment, endocrine therapy reduces the risk of recurrence. In advanced disease, the aim is to control cancer and symptoms. Your setting determines the duration and follow-up.
patient.indication_text: Exemestane is used for selected postmenopausal hormone-sensitive breast cancer after surgery, as extended endocrine treatment or for advanced disease after earlier treatment. The team checks which previous endocrine medicine you received and why a switch or extension is appropriate. If switching after tamoxifen, the earlier years count towards the intended total treatment plan.
patient.administration_text: Swallow the tablet whole, preferably after a meal; do not chew or crush it. Skip a missed dose and continue at the next scheduled time; do not double the dose.
patient.monitoring_summary: FBC, renal and liver profile, confirmation of menopause when uncertain, and bone / fracture assessment. Consider baseline vitamin D as specified by the product information. The NICE adjuvant baseline-DXA recommendation has an exception for patients already receiving adjuvant bisphosphonates. Review symptoms, adherence and bone health. Repeat bone density and lipids when indicated; assess other blood tests according to the clinical plan.

agents.mechanism: Reduces the oestrogen available to stimulate cancer cells
agents.explanation: Exemestane switches off aromatase, the enzyme that makes oestrogen in tissues after menopause. This reduces the hormone signal that can encourage hormone-sensitive breast cancer cells to grow. The body makes new enzyme over time, so tablets must still follow the prescribed daily schedule. It does not reliably switch off functioning ovaries; any ovarian suppression must be prescribed and checked separately.

items.title: Who this information covers
items.text: Exemestane is used for selected postmenopausal hormone-sensitive breast cancer after surgery, as extended endocrine treatment or for advanced disease after earlier treatment. The team checks which previous endocrine medicine you received and why a switch or extension is appropriate. If switching after tamoxifen, the earlier years count towards the intended total treatment plan.

items.text: FBC, renal and liver profile, confirmation of menopause when uncertain, and bone / fracture assessment. Consider baseline vitamin D as specified by the product information. items.title: Heart checks
items.text: ECG or other heart tests depend on symptoms and personal risk; this medicine alone does not require a routine HER2-style echocardiogram schedule.

items.title: Bone health
items.text: Offer baseline DXA when starting an adjuvant aromatase inhibitor if not already receiving adjuvant bisphosphonates; assess fracture risk and relevant previous results. Under the 2025 joint guidance, patients with a T-score above −2.0 and no additional risk factors generally have risk and bone density reassessed every one to two years. Patients on bone-protective treatment generally have BMD reassessed about every two years. Fracture, substantial bone loss or a change in risk can require earlier review. The clinician selects the interval and any bone treatment; these are not automatic yearly scans for everyone.

items.title: Early-breast follow-up
items.text: After curative treatment, annual mammography is generally used for remaining breast tissue: both breasts after conservation or the opposite breast after unilateral mastectomy. The mastectomy side is not routinely mammographed. Routine CT, bone scans and tumour markers are not recommended for asymptomatic early-breast surveillance. New symptoms need assessment between appointments.

items.title: Surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy
items.text: In an early-breast pathway, chemotherapy, if indicated, precedes endocrine treatment. Surgery and its pathology guide adjuvant choices. Postoperative radiotherapy is usually delivered after recovery and any adjuvant chemotherapy; aromatase inhibitors may overlap radiotherapy under the agreed plan. Tamoxifen timing around radiotherapy is agreed by the treating teams. None of these additional treatments is automatically required by an endocrine prescription.

items.title: Advanced-disease scans
items.text: For advanced breast cancer, response assessment is generally every two to four months, adapted to disease pace, sites, symptoms and treatment. Indolent disease may be reviewed less often; new symptoms can prompt earlier scans. The team chooses the imaging method; this is not a universal three-month CT chest/abdomen/pelvis order.

items.title: Tumour markers
items.text: Tumour markers may supplement imaging and clinical assessment in advanced disease if they are informative, especially if elevated at baseline. They do not replace scans, and a marker change alone should not determine treatment failure. There is no universal fixed marker timetable.

items.title: Menopause, pregnancy and contraception
items.text: Confirm the postmenopausal endocrine state. Any ovarian-suppression combination needs a separate prescription and monitoring plan.

questions.q: How long will treatment continue?
questions.a: If you switch after tamoxifen, the earlier years count towards the intended total endocrine course. Switching does not automatically mean starting a new full course. The team confirms your intended total and whether a later extension is appropriate. Advanced-disease treatment continues according to benefit and tolerance.

questions.q: Do I need a port or home pump?
questions.a: No port or home infusion pump is needed for this medicine itself. Any separately prescribed medicine has its own access requirements.

questions.q: Can I use HRT, vaginal oestrogen or supplements?
questions.a: Check with the oncology team before starting any hormone-containing treatment, including vaginal oestrogen, or any new medicine or supplement. Some can oppose this treatment or change how it works. The team can suggest symptom treatments and decide whether specialist review is needed.

questions.q: What if periods return or menopause is uncertain?
questions.a: Tell the team promptly about a return of periods or new vaginal bleeding. No periods after chemotherapy does not always mean the ovaries have permanently stopped working. Hormone blood tests may be needed. Ovarian suppression, if prescribed, has its own schedule and monitoring.

questions.q: What should I do if symptoms make tablets difficult to continue?
questions.a: Tell the team early about joint pain, hot flushes, sleep, vaginal or sexual symptoms, fatigue or missed tablets. Support, a supervised break or a change of medicine may be possible. Agree the plan with the prescriber rather than changing or stopping treatment yourself.

questions.q: Can another medicine make exemestane less effective?
questions.a: Yes. Some medicines for seizures or infections, and St John’s wort, can reduce its effect. Check every new prescription, over-the-counter medicine and supplement with the oncology pharmacist. Do not compensate by taking extra exemestane.

questions.q: Do I need calcium and vitamin D?
questions.a: The NCCP regimen advises daily calcium and vitamin D supplementation. Ask the team or pharmacist to confirm the suitable product and dose, taking account of your diet, blood results, kidney health and any supplements you already take. Bone-protective medicines and bone-density checks follow your individual fracture-risk plan.

evidence.applicability: Defined adjuvant tamoxifen-to-exemestane switch. Advanced disease after tamoxifen failure, not an adjuvant trial.
evidence.qualitative_result: IES: long-term follow-up after switching from tamoxifen to exemestane: In ER-positive/unknown disease, 10-year BCFS absolute difference was 4.0 percentage points (95% CI 1.2–6.7); HR 0.81 (0.72–0.92), favouring the switch. Overall survival in that analysis was not statistically significant: HR 0.89 (0.78–1.01; P=0.08), absolute difference 2.1 percentage points (−0.5 to 4.6). Exemestane versus megestrol after tamoxifen failure in advanced breast cancer: Median time to progression was 20.3 versus 16.6 weeks (P=0.037), favouring exemestane. patient.title: Capivasertib + fulvestrant
patient.context_label: Gene-altered, ER-positive / HER2-negative advanced breast cancer
patient.schedule_label: Four days on / three off, with fulvestrant injections
patient.schedule_summary: Capivasertib is taken twice daily for four days, then stopped for three days, each week. Fulvestrant injections are given on Days 1 and 15 of the first 28-day cycle, then Day 1 of later cycles. Treatment continues while helpful and tolerated.
patient.purpose: This combination aims to control advanced breast cancer. Capivasertib blocks a growth signal inside cancer cells and fulvestrant reduces signalling through the oestrogen receptor. Tumour testing helps identify people whose cancer has a relevant pathway alteration.
patient.indication_text: For adults whose ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer has a PIK3CA, AKT1 or PTEN change and has grown during or after hormone treatment. The team also checks general health and earlier treatment.
patient.administration_text: The usual starting capivasertib dose is 400 mg twice daily, about 12 hours apart, on the prescribed dosing days. Swallow tablets whole, with or without food; avoid grapefruit. Your prescription may use a lower dose. Each usual 500 mg fulvestrant dose is two slow injections into muscle, one in each buttock; no IV port or pump is required.

chapters.title: The treatment being discussed
chapters.intro: This combination aims to control advanced breast cancer. Capivasertib blocks a growth signal inside cancer cells and fulvestrant reduces signalling through the oestrogen receptor. Tumour testing helps identify people whose cancer has a relevant pathway alteration.

items.title: Who this regimen covers
items.text: For adults whose ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer has a PIK3CA, AKT1 or PTEN change and has grown during or after hormone treatment. The team also checks general health and earlier treatment.

items.title: Taking the tablets
items.text: Take capivasertib with or without food and swallow the tablets whole with water. Do not chew, crush, split or dissolve them. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice.

items.title: Injection visits
items.text: 500 mg intramuscularly as two 5 mL injections, one in each buttock, slowly over 1–2 minutes per injection. Cycle 1: days 1 and 15. Cycle 2 onward: day 1 of each 28-day cycle.

items.title: Ovarian suppression and pregnancy
items.text: If you are pre- or perimenopausal, a separately prescribed medicine must suppress ovarian hormone production with this combination. The team may also consider this for men. Age alone does not confirm suppression. Discuss fertility, pregnancy prevention and breastfeeding. Follow the longer fulvestrant contraception advice: two years after its last dose for women; capivasertib advice for men extends sixteen weeks after stopping. Your team confirms the individual plan.

chapters.title: Glucose and other checks
chapters.intro: Some checks happen between injection visits. Agree who books them and who reviews the results.

items.title: Starting and continuing checks
items.text: Check blood count, kidney and liver function before treatment and each cycle. Check fasting glucose and HbA1c before starting. Fasting glucose is checked at weeks 1, 2, 4, 6 and 8, then monthly; ideally before the tablet dose on day 3 or 4 of a dosing week. HbA1c is checked every three months, with an extra week-4 check for diabetes, prediabetes or high baseline glucose. Diabetes, new high glucose or metformin initiation needs extra checks under a written plan.

items.title: If you already have diabetes
items.text: Check fasting glucose daily for the first two weeks, then as often as the team advises. An extra HbA1c is recommended at week 4 when diabetes, prediabetes or high baseline glucose is present.

items.title: If glucose rises
items.text: The team may arrange at least twice-weekly checks, including tablet-taking and tablet-free days, and ketone tests or specialist review. Follow the written plan; symptoms can need urgent assessment even without a very high reading.

items.title: If metformin is started
items.text: The team checks kidney function weekly for up to three weeks after metformin starts with capivasertib, then on Day 1 of each cycle. Existing diabetes treatment needs individual reconciliation.

chapters.title: Support between treatment visits
chapters.intro: Early reporting helps the team treat symptoms and review doses safely.

items.title: Diarrhoea plan
items.text: Have the agreed anti-diarrhoea plan available before starting. NCCP gives loperamide 4 mg at first onset, then 2 mg after each loose stool, up to 16 mg in a day. Increase oral fluids and contact the team promptly for severe or persistent diarrhoea, inability to drink, dizziness, reduced urine or palpitations. Secondary prevention can be considered for recurrent diarrhoea.

items.title: Skin plan
items.text: Report a new rash promptly. Use moisturisers and any antihistamine or cream prescribed for your symptoms. Do not start steroids or change doses without review.

items.title: Medicine review
items.text: Tell the team about every prescription, non-prescription or herbal product. New medicines can change capivasertib exposure and require a reviewed dose.

items.title: Cancer response
items.text: Your team agrees which scans or other tests you need and when, and reviews symptoms, treatment benefit and your priorities.

questions.q: What if I miss or vomit a capivasertib dose?
questions.a: If a capivasertib dose is late, it may be taken within 4 hours of its usual time, leaving at least 8 hours before the next dose. If more than 4 hours late, skip it and take the next dose at the usual time. Do not double a dose. If you vomit after a dose, do not take an extra dose; take the next scheduled dose at its usual time. Contact the team if vomiting continues or prevents fluids or medicines.

questions.q: Do the three tablet-free days also change my diabetes medicines?
questions.a: Follow the individual written plan from the oncology and diabetes teams. Glucose can fall on tablet-free days. Do not automatically stop or continue a changed diabetes dose without the agreed instructions.

questions.q: Do I need ovarian suppression?
questions.a: Pre- or perimenopausal women need a separately prescribed LHRH medicine with this combination. The team may also consider this for men. Age alone does not confirm suppression.

questions.q: What if the tablets are paused?
questions.a: Contact the team for a revised plan. Do not restart or increase capivasertib yourself, and do not assume a tablet pause cancels or resets the fulvestrant injection schedule.

questions.q: How long is treatment and how will benefit be assessed?
questions.a: There is no fixed number of cycles. The team reviews cancer symptoms, scans, tolerability and priorities, and continues or changes treatment accordingly.

items.title: Breast treatment context
items.text: Advanced breast cancer. This patient suite describes the breast setting; the source protocol also has other tumour indications with their own clinical context.

items.title: Schedule and duration
items.text: Carboplatin is infused on Day 1 of each 28-day cycle. The team selects the dose using the prescribed AUC and kidney function. Treatment continues while helpful and tolerated; there is no fixed breast course length.

items.title: How treatment is given
items.text: Carboplatin is given through a vein over about 30 minutes after blood and symptom review and prescribed anti-sickness medicines. The complete appointment takes longer. A cannula or existing line may be used; a port is not automatically required.

items.title: Off-label breast indication
items.text: Carboplatin for metastatic breast cancer is an off-label use under this Irish NCCP protocol. The treating team must explain this, obtain informed consent and follow local Drugs and Therapeutics Committee approval requirements.

chapters.title: Checks before and during treatment
chapters.intro: Every dose depends on the reviewed treatment plan and results.

items.title: Blood and symptom checks
items.text: Blood count, kidney and liver tests are checked before each cycle. The team confirms the kidney-function method, current AUC and previous dose changes. Report numbness, hearing changes, infection and bleeding. Extra blood-count checks on Days 13–15 and Day 21 in the first cycles check the lowest counts.

items.title: Heart and response checks
items.text: Kidney dosing, hearing and nerve review are central. Scans follow the consultant plan; no universal heart-scan schedule is specified.

items.title: Fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation before treatment if relevant. Carboplatin may affect periods and fertility, sometimes permanently. Do not breastfeed during treatment. Discuss reliable contraception and contact the team immediately if pregnancy is possible. The linked Irish SmPC advises effective contraception for women during treatment and at least 6 months afterwards; men should avoid fathering a child during treatment and at least 3 months afterwards. Confirm the actual product/local advice and any longer requirement from other medicines. Discuss low blood counts and sepsis, bleeding, nausea/vomiting, fatigue, kidney, hearing and nerve effects, and infusion allergy. Benefit is uncertain and alternatives depend on your cancer and priorities.

chapters.title: Support and safety at home
chapters.intro: Keep the written medicine and urgent-contact plan.

items.title: Preventing sickness
items.text: Take the prescribed anti-sickness medicines before treatment and on the following days, even if you feel well. Follow your own prescription and contact the team if nausea or vomiting is not controlled.

items.title: Blood counts
items.text: Keep blood tests and use the emergency contact for fever, chills or bleeding. Preventive growth-factor injections depend on individual risk.

items.title: Kidneys and other medicines
items.text: Tell the team about every medicine or supplement, especially treatments that affect kidneys, hearing or bleeding. Follow individual drinking advice.

items.title: Steroid and rescue plan
items.text: The anti-sickness plan may affect sleep, glucose and bowel symptoms. Confirm the exact doses and last day of each medicine; contact the team if symptoms persist.

items.title: Urgent contact
items.text: Contact the oncology emergency service immediately for fever or shaking chills, sudden illness, bleeding, new breathlessness, chest pain or severe allergy. Report reduced urine, hearing changes and new numbness promptly. Do not wait for the next visit.

questions.a: The breast source continues until cancer progression or unacceptable toxicity. The team agrees response reviews and continuation; the fixed course of a particular trial or another cancer type does not set your course.

questions.q: Do I need heart scans?
questions.a: These two carboplatin monotherapy protocols do not mandate routine heart scans. Tests are arranged when symptoms, other medicines or your individual risks make them appropriate.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be chosen
evidence.intro: In the TNT study of advanced triple-negative or inherited BRCA1/2-associated breast cancer, carboplatin was active, but did not outperform docetaxel in the full study population. The inherited BRCA1/2 subgroup responded more often to carboplatin. These findings help inform a treatment discussion; they do not predict an individual result.

evidence.interpretation: The team considers previous treatment, cancer features, health and your priorities. A response in a trial cannot guarantee benefit for an individual.

items.title: Schedule and duration
items.text: Carboplatin is infused on Day 1 of each 21-day cycle. The team selects the dose using the prescribed AUC and kidney function. Treatment continues while helpful and tolerated; there is no fixed breast course length.

items.title: How treatment is given
items.text: Carboplatin is given through a vein over about 30 minutes after blood and symptom review and prescribed anti-sickness medicines. The complete appointment takes longer. A cannula or existing line may be used; a port is not automatically required.

items.title: Blood and symptom checks
items.text: Blood count, kidney and liver tests are checked before each cycle. The team confirms the kidney-function method, current AUC and previous dose changes. Report numbness, hearing changes, infection and bleeding. Additional tests follow symptoms and the individual plan.

items.title: Heart and response checks
items.text: Kidney dosing, hearing and nerve review are central. Scans follow the consultant plan; no universal heart-scan schedule is specified.

items.title: Fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation before treatment if relevant. Carboplatin may affect periods and fertility, sometimes permanently. Do not breastfeed during treatment. Discuss reliable contraception and contact the team immediately if pregnancy is possible. The linked Irish SmPC advises effective contraception for women during treatment and at least 6 months afterwards; men should avoid fathering a child during treatment and at least 3 months afterwards. Confirm the actual product/local advice and any longer requirement from other medicines. Discuss low blood counts and sepsis, bleeding, nausea/vomiting, fatigue, kidney, hearing and nerve effects, and infusion allergy. Benefit is uncertain and alternatives depend on your cancer and priorities.

items.title: Preventing sickness
items.text: Take the prescribed anti-sickness medicines before treatment and on the following days, even if you feel well. Follow your own prescription and contact the team if nausea or vomiting is not controlled.

items.title: Kidneys and other medicines

items.title: Steroid and rescue plan

items.title: Urgent contact
items.text: Contact the oncology emergency service immediately for fever or shaking chills, sudden illness, bleeding, new breathlessness, chest pain or severe allergy. Report reduced urine, hearing changes and new numbness promptly. Do not wait for the next visit.
